zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: The typeset running header begins with A, not G. A pale handwritten G at its left appears to correct this printing error; that later mark is recorded here as a copy annotation, not substituted into the printed header.

zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: the supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510 (Hideyuki Ohshima; assisting developer Taichi Aida), CC BY 4.0, https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html, was consulted after independent scan reading. It is an attributed lexical aid; the BnF scan governs the transcription and the English notes are reviewer-authored.

lines.note: Gugo is equated with meshi, cooked rice. The gloss begins a usage restriction with He pala-; the preceding page's Gugo- is only its catchword and is not added to this headword.
Ura completes palaura, followed by de molheres. The dictionary describes this rice-word as women's vocabulary; that historical register attribution is retained.

runs.text: Renda que tem o Dairi particular

lines.note: Gugoriǒ denotes the Dairi's specially assigned revenue for his table. Dairi is a Japanese title inside a Portuguese sentence, not an additional headword.
The revenue specifically supplies rice for the ruler's table. This completes the connection between Gugoriǒ and the preceding word for cooked rice.
Guguan is glossed simply as ignorance. The guan spelling is retained without expanding or modernizing the historical syllable sequence.

runs.text: Gu-i. Vorocana cocoro. i, Vaga zonbun.

lines.note: Gu-i, literally a foolish mind or intention, is explained by waga zonbun, one's own opinion. The internal hyphen distinguishes separate gu and i syllables and must not be discarded as a line-end mark.
The Portuguese makes Gu-i a humble expression for my opinion. Deſi remains the printed spelling and spacing; the meaning is self-deprecation rather than condemnation of another person's view.
Gu ichi names five and an ace on dice. Portuguese as denotes the one-pip face; this is a dice combination rather than the ordinary Japanese counting sequence.
Gǔjen is paired with tamatama and glossed raro, rarely or occasionally. S. marks written usage; the caron belongs over u, not over either vowel of the Japanese synonym.
Gujǒ is waga fumi, my letter. The Portuguese begins the explanation of the humble speaking convention, which is completed below.
Com humildade completes the self-deprecating register note for Gujǒ. It is not a separate sense of carta.
Gumai is explained by orokani, kurashi and the synonym guchi, ignorance. Ig- starts the Portuguese noun on the next row; the punctuation between the Japanese paraphrase and synonym is preserved.
Norancia completes Ig-norancia. This is the continuation of Gumai's gloss and contains no omitted Japanese headword.
Gumi is described only as a certain fruit. The source's generic botanical statement is retained without importing a species name into either the transcription or the definition.
Gumô is another word for guchi, ignorance. The marked long o and the independent entry are retained despite the repeated Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: Não ſe vſa perſi ſoo, ſe não cõ-

lines.note: Gun is explained by Icuſa, warfare or an army. The damaged long-s shoulder appears detached above the following a; Icuſa, rather than the draft's Iculã, is the chosen reading from the surviving stem, shoulder and warfare context. This is a nonblocking glyph uncertainty. The following restriction says gun is used in compounds, not alone.
Poſto completes cõ-poſto. Ichigun and nigun illustrate one and two military units, with the Portuguese explanation of their personnel continuing below.

runs.text: mero de gente que tem hum eſquadrão, dous,

lines.note: Mero completes numero: the gloss concerns the number of people in one squadron, two, and so on. Its wording does not prescribe a fixed troop strength.
After closing the numerical examples, Gunbiǒ is introduced with the gloss soldiers. It remains on the same physical row after a paragraph mark.

runs.text: Hũa parte, ou comarca do rei-

lines.note: The next Gun is the administrative district, paraphrased as kôri in the historical spelling Couori. Rei- begins reino in the Portuguese geographical definition.

runs.text: no: não ſe vſa perſi ſe não.

lines.note: No completes reino. The entry again restricts use to combinations such as Ichigun and ni-gun; those forms are examples of counting districts.
Gun completes nigun, followed by &c. The row is an example continuation, not a third independent Gun headword.
Gunamecaxi gives the transitive verb for making something move or stir. Its ſu and aita principal forms are preserved as historical morphology; me- begins menear below.

runs.text: near algũa couſa como membro q̃ eſtà como mor

lines.note: Near completes menear. The example is a limb that is almost lifeless or slack; the scan has no visible hyphen after mor, so the original unmarked division before tal is retained.
Tal completes mortal from the unhyphenated preceding row; froxo adds slack or weak. These adjectives explain the sort of limb movement meant by Gunamecaxi.
Gunameqi is the corresponding intransitive action, moving or stirring in that manner. The principal forms u and eita are retained without modernizing the inflection.
The phrase Gunagunato ſuru gives the same action with an expressive adverb. The scan shows long s without an f crossbar, correcting furu; Idẽ abbreviates the repeated gloss.

runs.text: Agoureiro da guerra, que diz o dia

lines.note: Gunbai is described here as a military diviner who chooses an auspicious day. The source defines a person, not the modern familiar object sense of the commander's fan.

runs.text: em que ſe ha de partir, dar batalha, &c.

lines.note: The diviner chooses when to depart or fight a battle. This completes the role described under Gunbai, with the original &c. left unexpanded.
Gunbiǒ is ikusa no tsuwamono, soldiers or warriors. Enlargement shows tçuuamono, without the extra no in the draft tçuuanomono; the Portuguese confirms the military-personnel sense.
Gente de guerra completes the gloss soldiers or fighting people. It is continuing Portuguese text rather than another Japanese synonym.
Gunchô is a flock of birds, paraphrased as muragaru tori. The circumflex is visible in the headword; the revised crop also restores the full left edge of the capital G.
The example describes a flock's chirping filling the ears. The scan repeats Gunchô with a circumflex, not the draft's caron; michi continues into tari below.

runs.text: O bando de paßaros faz grande traqui

lines.note: Tari completes michitari, being filled. Portuguese traqui continues without a printed hyphen into nada; the absent terminal mark is not supplied merely because the word is divided.
Nada completes traquinada, the noisy bustle of singing birds in the ears. S. is the separate written-usage label, not part of the italic translation.
This Gunchǔ means loyal service in war, explained by ikusa no chǔxet. Final t is a checked ending in the Japanese synonym, not an incomplete Portuguese word.
Guerra completes the war-service definition. The independent S. marks the expression as written usage and is kept outside the italic gloss.
A second Gunchǔ means within a war or battle, from ikusa no naka. It is a separate homophone rather than a continuation of the loyal-service meaning.
Batalha completes the alternative Portuguese wording for war or battle. This short continuation belongs to the second Gunchǔ entry.
A third Gunchǔ is the interior of a district, paraphrased as kôri no naka in the printed Couorino form. The administrative sense of gun is distinct from the military sense above.
Ou parte do reino completes the district description. The entry concerns location within an administrative region, not service rendered to it.
Guncô denotes services in war, explained by ikusa no chǔcô. Both final o marks are circumflexes in the scan; the draft's caron in chǔcǒ is corrected.
Guerra completes the definition of military services. The following S. is the upright written-register label and remains distinct from the Portuguese sentence.
Guncocu denotes lands and kingdoms. The example begins Gunco-, with a visible terminal hyphen, and continues as the object of mauaru below.
Guncocu wo mawaru means travelling through many lands and kingdoms. The physical split Gunco-cuuo is retained rather than joining the original lines.
Reinos completes the travel example's Portuguese list. This is a body continuation, not a column catchword.
Gundai is a district administrator, paraphrased as kôri no dai. The print ends at comar without a hyphen; the crop is widened leftward to include the whole headword and outer-rule context.
Ca completes comarca from the preceding row, finishing the description of an administrator for a district of the kingdom. This is the last body row of column 1.

zones.label: Column 2 running header and printed page number

lines.note: Gundô is collective movement, paraphrased as muragari ugoku. The final consonant in vgoqu is q, matching the historical spelling of ugoku rather than introducing another g.
Many people moving together completes the definition. S. is the separate written-usage label, not part of the italic phrase gente junta.
Gunen is glossed by motomuru, seeking or desiring to attain something. The Portuguese alternative buſcar takes its qualifying phrase on the next row.
Com o deſejo specifies pursuit in desire. This completes the definition rather than asserting that the desired object has already been obtained.
Gungin is ikusa no jin, an army or military camp. The spelling gin is retained as printed, rather than normalized to the neighboring Gunjin form with a different meaning.
Gungǒ is paraphrased as Couorito gǒ, kôri and gô. The scan's t replaces the draft's r; the following Portuguese distinguishes two levels of territorial division, supporting the conjunction to.
The larger district is called Gun, a Japanese term visibly embedded in the Portuguese explanation. The row ends at ſome without a hyphen; the comparison with the smaller division continues below.
Nos completes ſomenos, describing the smaller territorial division called Gǒ. Gǒ is visibly upright within the Portuguese sentence, and its caron is retained.
Gunguio is a school of fish, explained by muragaru uo. The initial vuo is the historical spelling of fish, and pei- begins Portuguese peixes below.
Xes completes peixes. The example describes the school floating or moving at the surface of the waves; its Portuguese translation begins with O at the row end.

runs.text: cardume de peixe anda ao lume dagoa. S.

lines.note: The fish are at the water's surface, ao lume dagoa. The final S. is a written-register label, and the historical joined dagoa is preserved.
Gunguiocu denotes gathered jewels, paraphrased as muragaru tama. The Portuguese expression muitas pedras continues into preciosas on the next row.
Precioſas juntas completes the description of many precious stones together. This is a continuation of the collective jewel-name entry.
Guni names the two-and-five combination on dice. Its short gloss is a gaming use, distinct from the expressions with gu and the particle ni on the preceding page.
Gunin is an ignorant or foolish person, explained by orokana hito. Vt introduces the proverbial insect-and-fire comparison below.
The fool is likened to a summer insect flying into a fire. The printed Japanese sentence, including fini for hi ni, remains intact rather than being replaced with a modernized proverb.

runs.text: neſcio he como a borboleta do estio, que che-

lines.note: Portuguese describes a summer butterfly approaching the fire. Che- begins chegandoſe, and the insect's action continues below.

runs.text: gandoſe ao fogo voando, ſe queima. Enten-

lines.note: The flying insect approaches the fire and burns itself. Enten- begins the source's explanation of how the comparison is to be understood.

runs.text: deſe de hum cobiçoſo, ladrão, &c. que ain-

lines.note: Deſe completes Entendeſe. The source applies the comparison to a greedy person or thief, with ain- starting ainda across the break.

runs.text: da que ſabe, que o ande matar, toda via furta.

lines.note: Da completes ainda: the thief steals despite knowing he will be killed. Ande and toda via retain the source's historical spelling and spacing rather than being rewritten as modern Portuguese.

runs.text: Gente de guerra, ou multidão de ſol-

lines.note: Gunjei denotes fighting people or a multitude of soldiers. The final ſol- begins soldados and has a visible line-end mark.
Dados completes ſoldados. This short row finishes Gunjei's collective-military definition; no separate Japanese entry begins here.
Gunjen means before a war, explained by ikusa no mae. The example that follows concerns preparations before fighting, not a location at the front of a formation.
Gunjenni kate wo hakaru means calculating provisions before war. The Portuguese translation starts Antes da and continues with the necessary food supply below.

runs.text: guerra lançar conta ao mantimento que he neceſ

lines.note: The example concerns calculating the food necessary for the army before war. Neceſ continues into ſario without a visible terminal hyphen; no hyphen is supplied from the expected word.
Sario completes neceſſario, followed by enough provisions for so many people. S. is the written-usage label, distinct from the italic translation.
Gunjin is ikusa-gami, a war deity, compared by the Portuguese compiler to Mars. Cami is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese phrase Cami da guerra, rather than a second headword.
Guerra completes the war-deity gloss. The parenthesis and o homem at the right belong semantically to the next entry's exclusion of humans, but their displaced physical position is preserved.

Gunjǒ is defined as all sentient living beings except humans. The excluded o homem is printed at the previous row's right edge, already represented by named displaced spans rather than silently moved here.

runs.text: Cortinas que ſeruem no exercito eſ-

lines.note: Gunmacu denotes military curtains or screens. The Portuguese describes their use in an army, with eſ- beginning eſtendidas on the next row.
The screens are stretched out bearing a painted emblem. Gunma- then begins the Japanese example, preserving the visible hyphen at the edge.
Cuuo faru completes gunmaku wo haru, stretching out the military screens. The Portuguese repeats the action with eſtender eſtas cortinas.
Gunnai means inside a district, paraphrased as kôri no uchi. The Portuguese construction Dentro de hum takes its district noun on the next row.

runs.text: Gun. i, Certa comarca do reino.

lines.note: Gun completes the Portuguese phrase inside a Gun, followed by an explanation of the district. In this occurrence Gun and the explanatory i are visibly italic; the embedded term is nevertheless marked for optional human font review.
This Gunome is a kind of hide or leather. The gloss does not specify the processing method or animal, so neither is supplied.
The separate Gunome denotes the five pips on dice. Itẽ is the Portuguese editorial word Item, not Japanese iten; its italic type and abbreviation mark are retained.
Permet. introduces a figurative extension of the dice pattern; the scan supports final t rather than the draft's i. Gunomeni monouo ſuru illustrates making something in that pattern.

runs.text: algũa couſa com lauor, ou pintura de cinco

lines.note: The object has worked or painted ornament with five points. This is the Portuguese explanation of the Gunome-pattern example, continued below.

runs.text: quinas à maneira dos cinco pontos dos dados.

lines.note: The five points are arranged like the five pips of a die. The comparison completes the design description without imposing a modern technical decorative term.
Gunpacu, explained by ikusa no maku, is another military-screen word. The abbreviated q̃ introduces the relative clause describing these curtains.

runs.text: com adiuiſa de cada hum ſe eſtendem nos ran-

lines.note: Each screen bears its owner's emblem and is extended in the quarters. The abrasion within cada does not prevent reading the word; the line-end ran- is visibly divided before chos.

runs.text: chos onde ſe aloja o exercito. S.

lines.note: Chos completes ranchos, where the army lodges. S. is the separate written-register label following the completed definition.
Gunpen is the vicinity of the military camp, paraphrased as ikusa no hotori. The Portuguese junto do arrayal confirms the locative sense.
Gunpi describes a flock in flight, explained by muragari tobu. The abbreviated q̃ introduces the relative clause on the following row.
The birds fly together, completing the flock definition. S. is the written-use label rather than an italic part of the sentence.
Gunpǒ is explained by Gun and couori as parts or districts. These are Japanese synonyms, not terms syntactically embedded in the Portuguese gloss.
Do reino completes the district definition, with S. marking written use. The signature and lower-right Gun- below this row are page furniture, not additional body lines.
